Day 82 of 100 · Kubernetes

Kubernetes Production Deployment

#100DaysOfCloudAndSecurityKubernetesPublished artifact recovered

The Kubernetes capstone connected scope, configuration, secrets, controllers, probes, networking, storage, ingress and Helm into one production-style deployment flow.

Architecture / mental model

Client → Ingress → Service → Ready Pods
                          ↙    ↓    ↘
                  ConfigMap  Secret  Persistent Storage
Helm → configurable release of the resource set

How it works

Each resource has a separate responsibility: Namespace scopes namespaced objects, ConfigMap carries non-sensitive configuration, Secret carries sensitive configuration, Deployment manages replicas/rollouts, Service provides stable routing, PVC requests storage and Ingress describes external HTTP/HTTPS routing.

Readiness decides whether a Pod should receive normal Service traffic; liveness addresses whether a container should be restarted. Treating those probes as synonyms can turn a transient dependency issue into an avoidable restart loop.

Helm packages the objects into a release, but release status is not end-to-end verification. The real client path must still be tested through Ingress, Service, endpoints and Ready Pods.

Hands-on reference

helm upgrade --install web ./web-chart --namespace prod --create-namespace --wait --timeout 5m
kubectl get pods -n prod
kubectl get svc -n prod
kubectl get ingress -n prod
kubectl get endpointslices -n prod

Verification

Deploy the release, inspect resource readiness, then issue a real client request through the ingress path. When traffic fails, validate Ingress → Service → EndpointSlices → Ready Pods rather than stopping at Helm status.

Field note / gotcha

`Running` does not mean `receiving traffic`. A Pod can be running while readiness fails, a Service selector can match no usable endpoints, and `helm --wait` still does not test the real client request path.

Security considerations

Review RBAC, Secret storage/encryption, Pod privilege, ingress exposure, TLS, NetworkPolicy and persistent-data controls as one connected system.

What I learned

A green Helm release is not an application-level health certificate; sadly, software refuses to respect our optimism.
